*Haṭharatnāvalī* by Śrīnivāsayogī.
Critical Edition by M.L. Gharote, Parimal Devnath, and Vijay Kant Jha.
Starting point:
HP; Ending point: Haṭhatattvakaumudī? — 4 types of Yoga (mantra, etc.)
Haṭha consists of 84 postures (āsanas), 8 breath-retentions (kumbhakas)—plus a ninth, the *bhujaṅgakaraṇī*—8 practices (kriyās), and 10 seals (mudrās).
Chapter One:
Having bowed to the illustrious Ādinātha, the high-minded Śrīnivāsa [spoke].
It bears the Haṭharatnāvalī as an ornament upon the necks of yogins. 1.1.

He is a moon in the ocean of the jewels of logic (*nyāyaratnārṇavendu*) regarding the Vedas, the Vedānta scriptures, the grammar composed by the Lord of Serpents (*phaṇipati*), his own treatises, the Tantras, the Prābhākara school, and that which was propounded by Kaṇabhuj (*kaṇabhuk*).

In the Sāṃkhya school of the Sārasvata lineage, which holds various philosophical views, the illustrious Jyotirvid—who knows the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*—the son of Agra-sara-rata, shines forth as Śrīnivāsa. 1.2.
Indeed, Gorakṣa, Matsyendra, and others understand the science of Haṭha;
likewise, Śrīnivāsa himself, though delighting in the Self, understands it.
[This is for those] who, due to delusion, remain in the thick darkness of many esteemed paths and do not know Rājayoga.
The science of Haṭha is taught solely for the sake of Rājayoga.
(1.4) Now, therefore, this first treatise on the inquiry into Yoga has been composed to state the subject matter and the purpose of Yoga within the science of Yoga. (1.5)

Furthermore, some wise ones declare that this very union of the inhaled and exhaled breaths, as well as of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), is indeed the purpose of yoga. 1.6.
The cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, however, is proclaimed as Mahāyoga.
Yoga is said to be fourfold by those who know yoga, and it bestows all perfections. ||1.7||
Mantrayoga, layayoga, and rājayoga as the third;
haṭhayoga shall be the fourth, bestowing liberation upon living beings. 1.8. Now, regarding mantrayoga:
Having assigned the mantra to the limbs and reciting the primary mantra, the wise practitioner shall become accomplished by whatever means; that is called Mantrayoga.
(1.9) Now, Layayoga:
Layayoga arises from the dissolution of the mind through conventional signs;
however, Ādinātha has declared that there are one and a half crores of such dissolutions.
The supreme convention is said to consist merely in fixing the gaze between the eyebrows.
In meditation on the posterior part of the head, one becomes the supreme conqueror of death (mṛtyuñjaya).
This very view is also accepted in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"May the methods of dissolution numbering one hundred and twenty-five million, taught by the venerable Ādinātha, be victorious!"
We consider the very practice of following the *nāda* (the inner sound) to be the most venerable among all methods of dissolution (*laya*).
Regarding the statement "dissolution, dissolution," what is the defining characteristic of dissolution?
The state of non-rebirth, dissolution, and the forgetting of sense objects. ||1.13||
[Regarding the state of non-rebirth— P] Now, as for the Royal Yoga (rājayoga):
there are no visible signs, no mental fluctuations, no restriction of place or time, and no suppression of the vital breaths.

When *rājayoga* is fully developed, there is no longer any exertion in *dhāraṇā* or *dhyāna*. (1.14) For those whose minds are stabilized in the illustrious *rājayoga*, having abandoned all notions of "I" and "mine," there is neither waking nor the state of deep sleep, neither life nor death, nor even the mind. (1.15)
Without Rājayoga, the earth does not shine; without Rājayoga, the night does not shine; even a manifold mudrā does not shine without Rājayoga. (1.16)
The seats, the various and divine potations (kumbhakas), and the methods (karaṇas)—even the practice of Haṭha with its limbs bestows the fruit that is Rājayoga. 1.17.
Now, Haṭhayoga:
The ten [practices] beginning with Mahāmudrā, the eight activities, the kumbhakas, and the eighty-four postures—they call this by the name "Forceful" (dhaṭha). 1.18.
Without Haṭha there is no Rājayoga, and without Rājayoga there is no Haṭha;
the pervasion of Śrī Rāja-yoga and Haṭha-yoga is inseparable. (1.19)
According to another view:

"The letter *ma* is said to be the mind (*manas*), and the letter *tra* is called the vital breath (*prāṇa*). From the union of mind and breath, yoga indeed receives the designation of 'mantra'. (1.20)
Having drawn back the function of the apāna, the prāṇa moves into the middle [channel];
it shines in the lotus of the sky, and for that very reason, it is indeed called Rājayoga.
By the syllable *ha* the sun is expressed, and the syllable *ṭha* is designated as the moon;
when the moon and sun have become equalized, *haṭha* bestows the ultimate reality.
Even one who is old, diseased, or weak becomes young again.
Through practice, one who is untiring attains perfection in all yogas.
At the initial stage of practice, a diet of milk and similar foods is recommended;
once the practice has become firm, there is no such restriction regarding food.
At the first stage of practice, phlegm and the other humors overflow; through the state of engaging in improper actions, all diseases will arise. (1.25)
In this regard, we shall describe the eight practices beginning with *cakrī* according to the tradition of our guru:
*cakrī*, *nauli*, *dhautī*, *netī*, *basti*, *gajakaraṇī*, *trāṭaka*, and *mastakabhrānti*; these are declared to be the eight practices. (1.26)
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Dhauti, basti, as well as neti, trāṭaka, naulika, and kapālabhrānti—these are declared to be the six karmas. (1.27) [HP 2.22]

This view must be considered: how could it be possible in the absence of the *cakrī*? Because it contradicts the intended object, this view is inconsistent. The effort to refute the criticisms stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*, however, merely imitates the breaking of a body with towering peaks. Enough with striking an axe at what can be cut by a fingernail; let us desist.
This eightfold ritual action, which effects the purification of the jar, must be kept secret;
it should never be told to anyone, just like the sexual union of a woman of noble family.
Now, the practice of *cakrikarma*:
having extended the anal canal, one should rotate the fingers fearlessly until the anus becomes dilated; this is declared to be *cakrikarma*. (1.29)

By the practice of *cakrī*, the root disease of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and the condition of great enlargement of the abdomen (*mahodara*) are destroyed, and the purification and stimulation of the bodily wastes (*mala*) are brought about. (1.30)

The purification of impurities and the illumination of all ritual actions is proclaimed by me as the practice of the wheel (*cakrasādhana*). However, for those lords who delight in their own self, the practice of the wheel is not approved. (1.31)
That should be performed by practitioners for the sake of accomplishing all rites; therefore, it should be understood by the best of yogis precisely according to the method I have explained. 1.32.
Now, as for *nauli*:
that *nauli* is said to be of two kinds, namely *bhārī* and *ekāntarā*.
The *bhārī* occurs by way of the external form, while it likewise arises within. (1.33)
Bending the shoulders, one should whirl the abdomen from left to right with the force of a powerful vortex;
this is *nauli*, which is praised by the Gauḍas. (1.34)
This *nauli*, the crest-jewel of *haṭha* practices, is always a source of bliss that kindles the digestive fire, promotes digestion, and so forth; it dries up all defects and diseases. 1.35.
Now, the internal [practice]:

By means of the *iḍā* with the force of its circulation, and likewise by the *piṅgalā*, one should cause [the breath] to revolve through both; this has indeed been described by me as occurring within.
Now, regarding *dhauti*:
a washed cloth, twenty cubits in length and four fingers in width, having been well-soaked, one should slowly swallow it. (1.37)
Then one should withdraw this [air]; through practice, this is called *dhauti*.
By doing this day after day, the digestive fire of the stomach increases. (1.38)
Cough, asthma, splenic disorders, leprosy, and the twenty diseases of phlegm—by the power of the practice of *dhauti*, these indeed run away; of this there is no doubt.
Now, the practice of *neti*:
The thread, resembling the tail of a rat and well-prepared with a smooth luster, measuring six spans in length, is the characteristic of the *neti* thread. (1.40)
Having inserted this [cord] into the nasal passage, one should gradually draw it out from the mouth;
having tied the end of the cord, one should rotate it between the nose and the passage.
Then one should perform churning; this is called "Neti" by the perfected ones (siddhas). 1.41.
The purification of the skull should be performed, which bestows divine vision;
furthermore,
this supreme gaze arises as the destroyer of diseases occurring above the collarbone.
Now, regarding enema (basti):
enema is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by water and air. Having prepared the apparatus according to one's capacity, one should likewise administer the enema. 1.43.
Having contracted the wind, one should release it into the abdomen through the anal canal;
this is called the vāyubasti. Now I shall describe the jalabasti. 1.44.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, with a finger inserted into the anal canal,
one should fill the abdomen through the anal canal by means of the path of the *cakri*.
Having performed the *vicitrakaraṇī*, one should exhale the water fearlessly;
having filled [the abdomen] to its full capacity, one should remain still for a moment and then release it. (1.46)
One practicing enema therapy must certainly not eat for three *ghaṭikās*.
Remaining in a windless place, self-controlled, and eating wholesome and moderate food, one should stay there. (1.47)
Whether it be abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, or disorders of wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth, they are indeed driven out by the power of the enema therapy; of this there is no doubt. (1.48)

The practice of the water enema (jalabasti), when repeatedly performed, bestows clarity upon the elements, the sense organs, and the internal faculties; it grants luster and the brilliance of fire, and destroys the entire accumulation of defects.
(1.49) Now, according to the view of the author of the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
Seated upon a high seat with the nozzle inserted into water reaching the navel, one should perform the contraction of the *ādhāra*;
that is the *kāpāla* enema practice (*bastikarma*).

However, for us, the contraction of the water by means of a nozzle inserted into the anus—considered in comparison to the methods of the enema practice belonging to the path of certain masters of yoga who follow a single tradition—is this very method, in which the path of the water enema is practiced by contracting [the sphincter] with a finger inserted into the anal nozzle; this appears to be the most appropriate method, as it is common to all masters of yoga such as Carpaṭi and others.
Now, regarding the *gajakaraṇī*:

while vomiting the substance within the stomach and raising the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) into the throat-pipe, it is called the *gajakaraṇī* by those who know *haṭhayoga*, due to the gradual mastery of the path of the vital air (*vāyu*). (1.51)
Alternatively—
having drunk water with sesame and jaggery up to the throat, or coconut water,
one should perform *kumbhaka* by holding the breath along with air and water in the path of the wind according to one's capacity.

Having completely purified it by means of the wind of the enema (basti-vāyu), this practice— whereby the water from a jar is drawn up through the throat-pipe by the trunk of a heavy elephant— is called "the heavy-elephant-trunk" (guru-gaja-karaṇī) by those who know Haṭha-yoga. ||1.52||
Just as the royal elephant shines among the herds of elephants, so indeed does the female elephant (gajakariṇī) stand preeminent among the Haṭha systems. 1.53
Now, regarding *trāṭaka*:
having gazed at a subtle object with a steady gaze while remaining concentrated, until tears begin to fall—this is what the teachers have called *trāṭaka*. (1.54)
Trāṭaka is the opener for eye diseases and the door-bolt against drowsiness and other ailments;
it should be guarded with effort like a casket containing jewels. (1.55) Now, the Kapālabhastrikā:
The bellows of blacksmiths consist of the rapid alternation of inhalation and exhalation;
this is known as the "skull-bellows," which dries up all diseases.
(1.56) Or else:
One should whirl the skull rapidly to the left and to the right;
through the application of exhalation and inhalation, this is called *kapālabhastrikā*.
It indeed destroys the disorder of phlegm and the water-born disorder of bile;
it purifies the skull and the wheel of Brahmā is cleansed. 1.58.
"It is purified"— these are the eight actions.
Emaciation of the body, clarity of the face, distinctness of sound, and purity of the eyes;

freedom from disease, mastery over the *bindu*, stimulation of the digestive fire, and purification of the channels—these are the signs of success in *haṭha*. [The eight types of karma] remove the grossness consisting of phlegm, fat, impurities, and so forth.
Then one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); it is accomplished without effort.
(1.60) The thorough purification of the six chakras is the cause of breath control;
it is the destruction of all diseases and the means for the path to liberation. (1.61)
One indeed attains bodily health through the power of the eightfold karma;
the purification of the support is performed by means of the wheel, and the purification of the sign by means of the vajrolī practice.
The Maṇipūra at the navel is reached by the practice called Nauli,
while the heart and the throat-cakra are reached by the practice called Dhauti.
Purification should be performed upon the command by means of the Neti and Trāṭaka practices;
purification of the entire body should be performed by means of the single practice of Basti and Bhastrā.
Through the practice of the bladder-bag (*bastibhastrikā*), there are the support (*ādhāra*), the self-supported (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), the jewel-purified (*maṇipūra*), the unstruck (*anāhata*),
the pure (*viśuddha*) located at the throat-wheel, and the command-wheel (*ājñācakra*) between the eyebrows at the face.
Knowing it as the breaking of the wheel, it is beyond the wheel and stainless. ||1.65||
In the virtuous land of Surāṣṭra, which is well-supplied with food and free from calamities,
the practitioner of Haṭhayoga should reside within a solitary hut.
[This hut] should have few doors, be without holes, pits, or uneven floors, and should be neither too high, nor too low, nor too long.
Cleanly smeared with thick cow dung, free from all defects,
beautiful with an outer courtyard, a raised platform, and a well, and surrounded by a wall—
this is said to be the characteristic of a yoga-maṭha by the Siddhas who practice Haṭha. (1.67)

Staying in such a monastery, free from all thoughts, one should always practice yoga alone by the path taught by the guru. (1.68) Abandoning sleep, moderate in diet, having conquered the breath and the senses, [one should practice].
The yogi who is constantly devoted to the practice of Haṭha becomes equal to Brahman. ||1.69||
O Pārvatī, those men on earth who revile the Lord of Yogis, Yoga itself, or the science of Yoga, are Rākṣasas.
Wondrous foods such as wheat, *śāli* rice, barley, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice; milk, clarified butter, cream, fresh butter, sugar, and honey;
the five vegetables consisting of ginger, *paṭola* fruit, leaves, and *japa*; divine beans such as mung beans; and water—these are the path of Yama and Indra.
Bitter, sour, pungent, salty, hot, and green vegetables; *sauvīra* vinegar, oil, sesame, mustard, fish, and wine; [these are the path of Varuṇa].
They say that the meat of unborn animals, curd, buttermilk, horse-gram, *kodrava* grain, oil-cakes, asafoetida, garlic, and the like are unwholesome.
(1.72) Likewise, there is the saying of Gorakṣa:
"One should avoid associating with the wicked, delighting in fire, women, and travel on roads."
Likewise, physical hardships such as bathing at dawn, fasting, and so forth [are taught].
Matsyendra’s statement also says:
"In the destroyer of fluids, the destroyer of death, the maker of gold, the destroyer of impurity, the destroyer of passion, and the remover of disease..."
In the fullness of the wind, in the fullness that bestows life, in the meditation on the self, in meditation that brings about liberation. ||1.74||

The yogi should partake of food offered to Śiva as an oblation (naivedya) that is excellent, well-seasoned, unctuous, derived from cow products, nourishing to the bodily constituents (dhātu), desired by the mind, suitable, reduced by one-fourth [of the usual amount], and dedicated to Śiva. (1.75)
This very person is one who eats in moderation, being entirely free from coarse food. ||1.76||

Excessive eating, over-exertion, excessive talk, adherence to restrictive rules, attachment to people, and fickleness—by these six, yoga is destroyed. (1.77) [But it is established] through enthusiasm, determination, fortitude, and the perception of the meaning of the knowledge of reality. (1.78)
Through the steadiness of the *bindu* which is motionless, through moderation in diet, through avoidance of contact with people,
through the abandonment of sleep, through mastery over the breath, through stability on the seat, and through freedom from laziness.
And through the grace of the Guru and the Teacher, yoga is accomplished by means of these. ||1.78||
And through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, and by the power of the practice of yoga.
But the perfection of yoga arises only through the grace of the Lord. ||1.79||
Śrī Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Śābara, Ānanda, Bhairava, Śāraṅgī, Mīna, Gorakṣa, Virūpākṣa, and Bileśaya;
[as well as] the yogi Manthānabhairava, Siddha, Buddha, and Kandalī.
Korandaka, Surānanda, Siddhipāda, and Carpaṭī;
Karoṭi, Pūjyapāda, Nityanātha, and Nirañjana.
Kapālī, Bindunātha, and he who is called Kākacaṇḍīśvara; Allama, Prabhudeva, Naiṭacūṭi, and Ṭiṇṭiṇi;
Bhālukin, Nāgabodha, and likewise Khaṇḍakāpālika.
These and other great Siddhas, by the grace of Haṭhayoga,
having shattered the staff of Time, roam about within the cosmic egg. (1.84)

I shall now describe the characteristics of the eight types of breath-retentions (kumbhaka). For the sake of attaining unprecedented and superior accomplishments, the wise person should practice these breath-retentions. 2.1.
Alternatively,
when the wheel of the channels has been purified by means of breath-restraints according to the rules,
the vital air enters easily, piercing the opening of the *suṣumnā*. (2.2)
When the middle *māruta* arises, stability of mind is produced;
that state in which the mind becomes perfectly steady is itself *manonmanī*. (2.3)
To achieve that, one who knows the method should always perform kumbhakas;
through the practice of various kumbhakas, one shall attain manifold accomplishments. ||2.4||
Bhastrikā, Bhrāmarī, Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, Śītalī, Mūrcchā, Sītkāra, Kevala—these are the eight types of Kumbhaka; with Bhujaṅgakaraṇī, the Kumbhakas are nine in number. ||2.5||
Alternatively, there are eight types of breath-retentions (kumbhaka): Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, Sītkāra, Śītalī, Bhastrikā, Bhrāmarī, Mūrcchā, and Kevala. 2.6.

At the end of inhalation (*pūraka*), the lock known as *jālandhara* should be performed; at the end of retention (*kumbhaka*) and at the beginning of exhalation (*recaka*), the *uḍḍiyāna* lock should be performed. By quickly contracting the lower [abdomen] when the constriction of the throat has been made, [the breath is held].
By means of the western posture, the vital breath (prāṇa) shall enter the central channel (brahmanāḍī).
Having raised the downward breath (apāna) upward and led the vital breath down from the throat,
the yogi becomes free from old age and attains the age of sixteen.
Now, the breath-retention known as *sūryabheda*: having slowly drawn in the external air through the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*),
one should cause it to reach from the throat down to the heart with a sound.
One should retain the breath as desired and then exhale through the *iḍā*;
one should also exhale the air slowly for the purification of the skull.
It purifies the skull, destroys wind disorders,
and eliminates worms; it also cures lethargy, subdues wind disorders, and kills worms and insects.
This practice, known as *sūryabheda*, is a form of *kumbhaka* that should be performed again and again.
Now, regarding *ujjāyī*: having restrained the mouth and slowly drawn the breath in through both nostrils...
Just as it reaches from the nostrils to the heart and throat, up to the heart, so does its own sound;
one should retain the breath as before and then exhale through the *iḍā*.
It is said to remove phlegm from the throat and increase the digestive fire of the body;
it destroys disorders of the channels, dropsy, and humors located in the tissues.
This kumbhaka known as ujjāyī should indeed be performed while walking or standing.
Now, regarding the sound *sīt*:
one should produce the sound *sīt* and likewise expel it through the mouth and the nose.
By means of such practice, one becomes a second Kāmadeva. (2.16)
To be served by the circle of yoginīs, he is the agent of creation and destruction;
neither hunger, nor thirst, nor sleep, nor even laziness arises.
He becomes one whose body acts according to his own will, free from all calamities.
By this method, the lord of yogis truly shines upon the earth.
(2.18) Now, as for *śītalī*:
having drawn in the breath with the tongue, following the previous *kumbhaka*...
The wise practitioner should slowly exhale the breath until it reaches eighty counts.
This practice called Śītalī Kumbhaka destroys abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, digestive imbalances, fever, bile, hunger, thirst, and poisons. (2.19–2.20)
Now, the bellows-breathing (bhastrikā), exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) consist of the syllable Om (praṇava).
Exhalation is the constant out-breath; inhalation is the cessation thereof.
That which is established in equanimity is proclaimed as *kumbhaka*.
Just as the bellows of smiths are moved with great force,
even so the wise man should move the vital air situated within his own body.
He should fill [the body] with the solar breath (*sūrya*) in such a way that exertion arises in the body.
Just as the belly becomes full, so too does it become light through the movement of air. ||2.23||
One should hold the breath firmly with the middle and index fingers, excluding the nose [tip],
having performed the *kumbhaka* as before, one should exhale the air through the *iḍā*.
It removes wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases the digestive fire of the body.
This practice called *bhastrā* (bellows), which destroys the obstructions such as phlegm located at the opening of the *brahmanāḍī*,
must be performed especially.
Now, the *bhrāmarī* (the humming bee):

Through the constant practice of yoga by the lords of yogis— [the breath] with a resonant roar during inhalation, the humming of a bee during retention, and the gentle sound of a female bee during exhalation— a certain play of bliss arises within the mind. (2.26)
[The Fainting of Bliss – ānandamūrcchā] Now,
at the end of the filling [of the breath], having firmly bound the *jālandhara* lock, one should slowly [proceed].
This [practice] called *mūrcchanā* causes the mind to swoon and bestows happiness. (2.27) Now, as for the *kevala*:
that which is the effortless retention of breath, having abandoned both exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*).

This is called *prāṇāyāma*; indeed, that is the *kevalakumbhaka* (the absolute retention). When *kevalakumbhaka*, devoid of exhalation and inhalation, is mastered, there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult for him to attain.

One who is capable of retaining the breath at will by means of the *kevalakumbhaka* alone—such a one is said to possess *rājayoga*; of this there is no doubt. (2.30) Now, the practice of becoming like a serpent (*bhujaṅgīkaraṇa*).
One should fill the breath through the throat and exhale it from the throat-passage;
this is known as the ninth kumbhaka, called Bhujaṅgīkaraṇa. ||2.31||
The great seal (mahāmudrā) is the great bond, the third being the great penetration;
Uḍḍiyāna is the root-bond, and the bond is named Jālandhara. ||2.32||

Karaṇī, that which is called Viparītā, Vajrolī, Śakticālana, [Mūlabandha], Jālandhara, Uḍḍiyāna, Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, and Khecarī according to the tradition—these are proclaimed as the ten mudrās. (2.33)
The mudrās proclaimed by Ādinātha bestow the eight sovereign powers;
they are beloved by all the Siddhas and difficult to attain even for the great. (2.34)
Thus have the ten mudrās been proclaimed by Śambhu, the primordial Lord.
Among them, each one individually is preeminent and bestows the great siddhis.
Now, regarding Mahāmudrā:
I shall explain Mahāmudrā as it was spoken by Vasiṣṭha out of his great affection. (2.36)
Pressing the vulva with the left foot and extending the right foot,
one should fill the mouth with both hands.
Having applied the binding at the throat, one should fill the breath from above;
just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff. ||2.37||
In that same way, the innate Kuṇḍalinī power becomes straightened.
Thus, that state of death arises, situated within the two petals.
Indeed, there is neither wholesome nor unwholesome food; even all tastes become tasteless.
Even if one has consumed terrible poison, it is digested as if it were nectar.
All disorders, headed by consumption, leprosy, constipation, abdominal tumors, and indigestion,
go to their destruction for one who practices the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
[Its defects are destroyed... This Mahāmudrā, which destroys old age and death, has been taught; it should be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone. (2.42)
Now, the Great Lock (mahābandha): one should place the heel of the left foot in the region of the perineum;
likewise, having placed the right foot upon the left thigh. (2.43) [HP 3.18]

One should fill the breath through the mouth, firmly pressing the chin against the heart; having restrained it and contracted the *yoni*, one should fix the mind in the center. One should exhale very slowly; this is called the *mahābandha*.
This yoga is the Great Lock (mahābandha), the bestower of all accomplishments;
having practiced it thoroughly on the left side, one should practice it thoroughly on the right side.
And this [central channel] awakens the upward movement of all the channels;
it maintains the confluence of the three rivers and leads the mind to Kedāra.
Just as a woman endowed with beauty and grace [is useless] without a man...
The great seal (*mahāmudrā*) and the great lock (*mahābandha*) are fruitless when devoid of penetration (*vedha*). [Now, regarding the great penetration:
The yogi, established in the great lock, having performed the inhalation (*pūraka*) with one-pointed mind...
Having drawn in the movement of the winds by means of the silent throat-seal,
this is performed eight times during every watch, day after day;
it accumulates a multitude of merits and always shatters the flood of sins.
Happiness comes first for those alone who possess right faith when there is no [other] means;
at the outset, one should avoid fire, women, and travel on the road.
With both hands joined together, one should gently strike the buttocks against the ground.
This very Great Piercing (mahāvedha) becomes the bestower of accomplishment through practice. || 2.51 ||
This triad is a great secret that destroys old age and death, increases the digestive fire, and bestows the qualities such as atomization (*aṇimā*). Now follows the *Uḍḍiyāna-bandha*:

Because the vital breath (*prāṇa*), when bound within the *suṣumnā*, is caused to fly upward (*uḍḍiyate*), it is therefore called "Uḍḍiyāna" by the practitioners of yoga. Since the great bird [of the breath] performs its flight (*uḍḍīna*) without ceasing, [it is so named]. (2.53)
That indeed is Uḍḍiyāna; therein the "bandha" (lock) is described.
One should maintain a backward tension in the abdomen above the navel;
for this is the Uḍḍiyāna bandha, the lion that destroys the elephant of death.
The Guru has declared that the innate (sahaja) state, even for the aged, becomes youthful;
it produces the external Ūḍyāṇa and increases external adornment. (2.56)
And as for Oḍḍiyāna, which is innate (sahaja), it has been taught by the Guru;
one should practice that without sloth, and even an old man shall become young again.
One should diligently perform the expansion [of the abdomen] either above or below the navel;
by practicing this for six months, one certainly conquers death—of this there is no doubt. (2.57) Now, the *mūlabandha*:
Pressing with the heel, one should contract the perineum and the anus;
by forcibly drawing the downward-moving *apāna* upward, this is called the *mūlabandha*. (2.58) [HP 3.60] It indeed makes the *apāna*, which moves downward, go upward by force.
Yogis call that contraction the *mūlabandha*;
indeed, by pressing the anus with the heel, one should forcefully contract the vital air.
Just as the vital breath repeatedly ascends further and further,
then, through the *mūlabandha*, the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, as well as *nāda* and *bindu*, attain oneness; at that time, one certainly attains the perfection of yoga— of this there is no doubt.

Through the constant practice of *mūlabandha*, there is a unification of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths and the cessation of urine and feces; even an old man becomes young again. When the *apāna* has moved upward and entered the sphere of fire (*vahni-maṇḍala*), [the state of mastery is attained].

Just as the blazing of a flame of fire is impelled by the wind, so too do the fire and the downward breath (apāna) move back and forth, possessing the nature of the root-form and the essential form [respectively]. [Then they move... the vital breath (prāṇa) possessing the nature of heat.]
By that, the fire born of the body becomes intensely inflamed;
struck by the staff, it surely attains straightness like a female serpent.
Then, as if having entered a bower, one should proceed into the interior of the *brahmanāḍī*.
Therefore, the root-lock (*mūlabandha*) must always be performed by yogis at all times. (2.65) Now, the *jālandhara* [bandha]:
Contracting the throat, one should firmly place the chin against the heart;
this is the lock known as Jālandhara, which destroys old age and death.
For it binds the network of channels; the water from the sky does not descend downward.
Therefore, when the constriction of the throat is performed, there is the Jālandhara bandha:
the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the wind become provoked.
This triad of bonds is supreme and practiced by the great Siddhas;
yogis know it to be the means of accomplishment for all Yoga Tantras. (2.68) When the constriction of the throat is quickly effected by contraction below, [the breath is held].
In the center, by means of the backward [movement], the vital breath (prāṇa) shall enter the channel of Brahmā (brahmanāḍī).
Having contracted the root-seat (mūlasthāna), one should perform the uḍḍiyāna lock;
having bound the iḍā and piṅgalā, one should cause [the breath] to flow along the western path.
By this very method, the vital wind (pavana) attains dissolution;
consequently, neither death nor old age, disease, and the like arise. (2.71) Now, the *viparītakaraṇī* [is described]:

Whatever nectar of divine form flows from the moon, the sun swallows it all; therefore, the physical body is perishable. In this regard, there exists a divine instrument for the sun that serves as a seal upon its mouth.
This is to be known through the instruction of the Guru, and not by means of millions of scriptural meanings.
(2.73) Above the navel and below the palate is the Sun; below the navel and above the palate is the Moon.
The practice called "the reversal" is obtained through the word of the Guru. (2.74)
The practice known as *viparītakaraṇī* destroys all diseases;
for one who is constantly engaged in its cultivation, it increases the digestive fire.
Indeed, the practitioner must provide himself with abundant food.
If the *alphāhāra* (the consumption of the alphabet) should occur, the fire would gradually burn the body.
On the first day, one should remain for a moment with the head downward and the feet upward.
And one should practice for even slightly more than a moment day after day.
Within six months, neither wrinkles nor grey hair are seen;
he who practices constantly for even a single watch (yāma) is a conqueror of time.
Even while remaining in a healthy state, one who is devoid of the restraints prescribed for yoga [should practice] the practice called *viparītakaraṇī*, as characterized by Śrīnivāsa. (2.79)
Now, regarding Vajrolī:
I shall describe Vajrolī, which is hidden by all yogins;
for it is an extreme secret and must not be given to just anyone.
Since it is equal to one's own life-force, one should certainly tell it only to that person;
even to one's own son, it must not be given except through the lineage of teacher and disciple.
The awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, the thorough purification of the channels, and the unification of Apāna and Prāṇa should be accomplished through the practice of Vajrolī. (2.82)
I shall describe the sequence of practice according to the tradition:
whether it be a woman or a man, the wise one should master the Vajroli. (2.83)
The wise one should proceed:
the *liṅga* suitable for blowing should be placed outside at the tip of the aperture [the phrase "phūtkārocitaliṅgarandhrāgre" appears in P, T, and t1].

First, the description of two tubes is undertaken: one is to be placed within the center of the aperture of the *liṅga*, and the other is joined [to it]. Between these two, the nature of the tube suitable for blowing is demonstrated.
One should not, even with great effort, fashion a tube out of gold, silver, copper, or iron that is suitable for producing a blowing sound. (2.84)
The tube, measuring twenty finger-breadths in length, beautiful, initially well-rounded and narrow,
resembling the form of a reed suitable for blowing, is used by those practicing forceful yoga (*haṭhayoga*).
[Is it "suitable for blowing" and "resembling the form of a reed"?]
One should carefully place that very same [substance] into the cavity of the *liṅga*;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the blowing (*phūtkāra*) so that the vital air may circulate. (2.85)
The author of the *Haṭhapradīpikā*,
however, with effort, performs a blowing through a reed-stalk into the vajra-cavity.
One should perform [this] very gradually for the sake of facilitating the movement of the vital air (vāyu).
The view of the author of the *Haṭhapradīpikā* regarding the practice of Haṭhayoga is a manifestation of ignorance and should therefore be disregarded.
If there were indeed a hollow reed [within], the wind would not circulate intensely;
therefore, the practice of circulating the wind is considered to be by means of a hollow reed and the like. (2.87)
The nature of the stalk (nāla) to be placed within the cavity of the liṅga is now described for the purpose of determining the dimensions of that cavity.
Like a thread, gold, a stalk, a serpent, or exceedingly pure copper— this is declared by the yogi Śrīnivāsa to be the substance of the stalk (*nāla*). (2.88)
One should fashion a lotus-shaped vessel out of three palas of silver, twelve finger-breadths in length; its stalk should be glossy, white, and soft.
Having directed [the breath], one should fearlessly place it for a moment within the aperture of the *liṅga*;
this brings stability to the *liṅga*, firmness to the *liṅga*, and increases great virility. (2.90)
The stalk, fashioned by the nāgas, was made of gold, exceedingly soft, and possessed of all its parts;
it was shaped like an umbrella, with three folds, and measured a span in length. (2.91)
One should carefully place the stalk, which is likewise measured by a span (vitasti), into the opening of the *liṅga*. ||2.92||
Immediately thereafter, an extremely firm *liṅga* arises;
once the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) has been established, it is forcibly drawn upward. (2.93)
Having placed a beautiful woman below in a secret place, naked,
while he himself becomes naked and lies upon her as she lies supine, both the woman and he indeed perform *kumbhaka* for a short while. (2.94)
A certain yogin should firmly embrace one another and insert the *liṅga* into the *yoni*.
He should cause it to enter.
Furthermore, one should perform mutual drinking from the lower lip and make sounds such as those from the throat. ||2.95||
One should scrape with the fingernail itself and retain what arises from perspiration;
by practice, one should draw upward the drop falling from a woman’s vulva.
And having drawn upward one's own displaced drop, one should preserve it.
In this way, one who knows yoga should protect the *bindu*; such a knower of yoga conquers death.
Death occurs through the falling of the *bindu*, while life arises from the retention of the *bindu*.
For human beings, semen is dependent upon the mind, and life is dependent upon semen.
Therefore, one must protect both the semen and the mind with great effort.
Thus, he who indulges with a woman should contemplate her alone in his mind.
In women, the menstrual blood residing in the womb is like vermilion.
Likewise, for a woman in her menses, one should protect both the menstrual flow and the seminal drop. ||2.100||
Just as the semen, being free from defects, enters the womb during the fertile period, so too does it attain oneness with the female blood through that very vital air (māruta). 2.101.
Lifespan, karma, wealth, and knowledge—this fourfold set is inscribed at the time of conception for the embodied being even while still in the womb. (2.102)
To whatever extent this body of the one dwelling in the womb is maintained, to that same extent the manifestation of this subtle body (liṅga) comes into being. (2.103)
If the drop (bindu) remains stable, one's lifespan increases eternally;
for the single drop is indeed the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (2.104)
From that, one becomes a master of royal yoga; it certainly does not happen otherwise.
Success does not come through mere consciousness alone, but indeed from the practice of the vital breath.
I shall describe the sequence of practice for women, proceeding very gradually.
Contracting the *liṅga* with both hands, one should cause the *maṇi* to enter within;
one should practice until the *maṇi* has entered. Thereafter, if she is capable, she should contract the *rajas* upward. (2.107)
Within her body, the sound (nāda) indeed attains the state of the drop (bindu).
Having unified that drop and that very passion (rajas), both produced from one's own body, [one should practice].
Through the practice of the yoga of *vajrolī*, the accomplishment of yoga rests in one's hand.
However, a woman should not practice *vajrolī* without knowing the science of yoga.
This yoga succeeds for those who possess merit, who are blessed, who are endowed with the truth, and who are free from envy; it does not succeed for those characterized by envy.
Of all yogas indeed, this yoga is the bringer of auspiciousness.
Therefore, this is the most excellent [path], bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||2.111||
A fragrant scent arises in the body of the yogin from the retention of the *bindu*. (2.112) Now, regarding the *sahajolī*:
the *sahajolī* and the *amarolī* are merely divisions of the *vajrolī*. (2.113)
Having placed auspicious ash produced from burnt cow dung into water,
one should apply it to the limbs of both the woman and the man after the *vajrolī* sexual union,
while they sit comfortably for a moment, free from all exertion.

This is called Sahajolī; it should always be practiced by yogis. (2.115) Now, having abandoned Amarolī—which is constant—and having abandoned the first flow because of its lack of essence, one should practice the final flow.

In the Kāpālika and Khaṇḍa traditions, the middle stream of nectar, which is cool and priceless, is practiced; [for] because of the predominance of bile, they abandon the first stream of water, and because of its lack of essence, they avoid the final stream. (Amṛtālī is thus practiced in the Kāpālika and Khaṇḍa systems.)
He who constantly drinks the *amarī* and performs it as a nasal drop (*nasya*) day after day,
and practices the *vajrolī* daily, is said to be a *amarolī*. (2.117) [Now follows the practice of *śakticālana*.]

Grasping the serpent by its tail, one should fearlessly awaken it; abandoning sleep, that power rises straight up forcefully, twelve finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in width. (2.118) = HP 3.107.
The characteristics of the wrapping cloth are described as gentle by those who know Haṭha;
then, having wrapped that tongue with the extended [cloth], the wise one [should proceed].
One should hold it firmly with both hands, using the thumbs and index fingers.
One should move it back and forth between the left and the right according to one's own capacity. (2.120)
For a period of two muhūrtas, he should move it fearlessly.
Drawing it slightly upward toward the Suṣumṇā which has entered the Kuṇḍalinī,
by this very movement for six months, his power (śakti) shall become upward-moving.
One should fill the breath with the Sūrya [mantra] and move it with the Sarasvatī [mantra].
By means of the movement within the womb of sound, the yogin is liberated from diseases;
he by whom the power (śakti) has been set in motion is a yogin who partakes of the supernatural attainments (siddhi).
What is the use of saying much more in this matter? He conquers death with ease, just as the Lord of Serpents is the support of the earth together with its mountains and forests.
For Kuṇḍalī is indeed the support of all the Yoga Tantras without exception;
she is the serpent, the coiled one, the female nāga, the wheel-bearer, the crooked one, and Sarasvatī.
Lalanā, rasanā, kṣatri, lalāṭī, śakti, and śaṅkhinī. ||2.125||
She is the rope, the female serpent, Śeṣā, Kuṇḍalī, the female snake, and the jewel.
The foundational power (ādhāraśakti) is Kuṭilā, Karālī, and the carrier of the vital breath (prāṇavāhinī). ||2.126||
She has eight faces, six supports, is all-pervasive, and is the bearer of creative ideation.
And thus, these well-known words are synonyms expressing the same meaning. ||2.127||
Thus ends the movement of the power (śakticālana); now follows the Khecarī.
And Khecarī is the final mudrā; it leads one to the aperture of Brahmā without delay.
Suṣumṇā, Amṛtā, Mūrdhā, and Lambikā are recorded as the designators [of the states].
Without the scripture there is no sequential order, and indeed without the sequential order there is no scripture.
Having understood the scripture endowed with its proper sequence, it is now being set forth for the illustrious ones on this earth. (2.129)
The scripture resembling the shape of a tongue is small, yet it is capable of cutting through that [tongue].
A wise physician should fashion an instrument resembling the leaf of the Snuhī plant for the purpose of applying forceps.
In the middle of the iḍā, the piṅgalā, and the suṣumṇā.
Having placed the index finger of the wisdom hand upon it, one should cut through the middle of the knot. ||2.131||
Two niṣkas, one niṣka, and half a niṣka [of] harītakī, ginger, and rock salt.
Having powdered that [substance], one should rub with that powder.
One should perform the movement of the śakti according to the method previously described.
Just as one would handle a milk-pail, so too should one practice the movement of power (śakti). ||2.133||
When seven days have passed again, one should cut off [the hair] the size of a sesame seed.
By means of the very sequence beginning with cutting, [the breath] should reach as far as the middle of the eyebrows.
For that long, the discourse of Śrīnivāsa should be carried out gradually.

In this regard, the tradition of Haṭhayoga holds that a child knows the past and the future through the *lambikā-yoga*. From the moment of birth until the fall from the womb, the tongue becomes bound in the *lambikā-yoga*. Due to the reflection of the *lambikā*, a subtle knot exists at the lower part of the tongue, which is still visible today to all men. It appears to me that it is precisely there that the breaking of the subtle knot which obstructs the *lambikā* must be accomplished.
In the chapter concerning the names of the Khecarīs proclaimed by the Supreme Lord, however:
The weapon was like the leaf of the Snuhī plant—extremely sharp, smooth, and stainless.
On the tongue that has been made even, one should cut away [the flesh] only to the depth of a hair;
for by cutting no more than a hair's breadth, the tongue does not become pendulous.
The intention of the authors in their hearts has been expressed by me. (2.137)
But Dattātreya, however...
The tongue has entered the hollow of the skull and is turned upward.
The gaze directed between the two eyebrows is the Khecarī mudrā.
For one who possesses it, there is neither disease nor death, neither sleep, nor hunger, nor thirst.
And there shall be no fainting for him who knows the Khecarī mudrā;
he is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tainted by karma.
And he who knows the Khecarī Mudrā is not afflicted by time. (2.140) [Haṭhapradīpikā 3.39, Vivekamārtaṇḍa 49]
One should gradually increase the digit (kalā) through the processes of cutting, moving, and milking.

As long as this [vital energy] touches the middle of the eyebrows, at that moment the siddhi of *khecarī* is attained. (2.141) Since there is an absence of an explanation regarding the method of piercing, [the opponent's position] is due to ignorance.
Because it is difficult to understand due to its use of common terminology, this doctrine should not be accepted. (2.142)
I shall now explain the convention according to the path shown by the Guru.
In the absence of the chain of conventional signs, how indeed could the Khecarī [mudrā] exist? (2.143)
It has the form of a serpent, is adorned with bracelets, and is attended by two chains.
Together with the crucible, it is six spans in length; this is the conventional definition.
The supreme [form] is fashioned from two chains, resembling a serpent and provided with rings and skull-cups.
They know the very long [tongue] to be twenty finger-breadths in measure, which brings about the emergence of the uvula. ||2.145||
And one should insert the tongue into the ring of the chain.
Just as one may enter the suṣumnā, so does one become a khecarī.
When the sealing by Khecarī Mudrā has occurred, the embodied being does not abandon the body.
Having cast off the body at the end of the eon, he goes to the abode of Brahmā.
When the vital breath has entered the Suṣumṇā, the sound is heard in eight ways.
It resounds like the noise of bells, drums, conchs, lutes, and flutes.
Tanūnapāt (Agni), whose radiance is like lightning, the sun, and the wind. || 2.148 ||
And by the Nāgas beginning with Vāsuki, or again by Takṣaka;
The poison is unable to take effect within the body of a yogi who has been bitten. (2.149)
And whoever should drink the pure nectar of the stream, which possesses the beauty of surging waves;
That yogi, whose body is as delicate as a lotus stalk, remains free from defects and lives for a long time.

(2.150) If the tongue, dripping with the essence of rasa, constantly attends to the tip of the uvula, then that [essence]—though resembling salt, pungent, bitter, and milk—is like honey and clarified butter. (2.151)
And from the openings of all the channels without exception, it has entered the tip of the tongue.
By whatever path one performs [this], one shall attain the lunar digit. ||2.152||

The accomplishments (siddhis) such as the discourse on mining, the discourse on [subterranean] cavities, the discourse on alchemy, and the discourse on elixirs arise for the yogins; among these, there are the Vajrī, the Lī, and the Khecarī.
There are also the Trikaṭumbī, the Haṭhā, the Golīḍha, and likewise the Śikhara.
The thirty-spoked vajra marked with the syllable Oṃ is above the navel; it is at the mouth of the two eyebrows. ||2.154||
Piṅgalā, Dambhinī, Sūryā, Yamī, and likewise Kākṣarā.
Kālāgni, Rudrī, and Caṇḍī—these shall be known by the name Piṅgala.
Iḍā, Candrā, Sinīvālī, Gaṅgā, and Cāmarabodhitā.
The words denoting Iḍā have been proclaimed in succession. ||2.156||
The tongue is denoted by the word "go" (cow), for its entry is indeed into the palate (tālunī).
The eating of beef, moreover, is the destroyer of great sins;
one should constantly eat beef and drink the wine of the immortals (amaravāruṇī).
I consider him to be of noble birth, while others are indeed destroyers of their lineage;
for [the world] is truly raised up by the fire produced from the entry of the tongue.
The essence that flows from the moon is that which is Amaravāruṇī.
Thus ends the second instruction in the *Haṭharatnāvalī*, as compiled by Śrīnivāsa Yogin.
The Third Instruction:
Now, the Eightfold Yoga.
Hereafter, the essential nature of the eight limbs of yoga is briefly described.
Many yogins have attained perfection through these excellent limbs. ||3.1||
Clarity and contentment of mind, silence, and restraint of the senses.
Compassion, courtesy, faith, uprightness, gentleness, and forgiveness. (3.2)
Purity of being, non-violence, celibacy, mindfulness, and fortitude.
And other such rules for bestowing honor are recorded in the Smṛtis. 3.3.
Bathing, purification, righteousness, truthfulness, recitation, fire-offerings, and libations;
Austerity, self-restraint, forbearance, prostration, and circumambulation.
And observances such as vows and fasts are known as physical restraints (niyamas). ||3.4||
Since it is the first limb of Haṭha, I shall now demonstrate Āsana.
One should practice that posture which brings stability, health, and flexibility of the limbs.
(3.5) [This was taught] by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and by yogins such as Matsyendra.
I perceive that certain seats have been taken by each single living being among the eighty-four hundred thousand [species]. (3.6)
Having extracted [the essence], eighty-four seats (pīṭhikās) were proclaimed by Śambhu.
Among those eighty-four seats, I shall describe the characteristics of some.
The sacred seats (pīṭhas) proclaimed by Ādinātha bestow bodily health and happiness. (3.8)
The Siddha, the Bhadra, the Vajra, and the supreme Siṃha-śilpāsana.
The hands are bound together in the hollowed-cup gesture (saṃpuṭita), forming four pure lotuses. ||3.9||
The *daṇḍapārśva*, the *sahaja*, the *bandhapiṇḍa*, and the *mayūraka*—the single-footed *mayūra* and the six-footed *mayūra* are described here. (3.10)
The Bhairava, Kāmadahana, Pāṇipātra, and Kārmuka postures;
the Svastika, Gomukha, Vīra, Maṇḍūka, and Markaṭāsana. (3.11)
Matsyendra, Pārśvamatsyendra, and likewise Baddhamatsyendra;
The state called Candra is without support, and Kāṇṭhava consists of a single foot. ||3.12||
The western expansion is the lord of serpents, possessing the western expansion of one who lies asleep.
This is the practice known as Citra, the shaking of Yoganidrā.
Beyond this, in the practice called Haṃsa-pādapīḍana, [the breath] reaches the surface of the navel.
The sky is the surface of the footstool, with the navel as its lovely footrest. ||3.14||
The scorpion posture, known as the wheel, is called the leap.
The tortoise on its back, the tortoise, and the bound tortoise—none of these are upright.
They call this the Kabandha posture, and also the Gorakṣāsana.

The *aṅguṣṭhamuṣṭika* (thumb-fist) posture is to be known, as well as the *brahmaprāsādita*. [3.16] The *pañcacūli*, the *kukkuṭa*, and the *ekapādakakukkuṭa*; the *ākārita*, the *bandhacūli*, and likewise the *pārśvakukkuṭa*. [3.17]
And these two, Ardhanārīśvara and Bakāsanadhara, carry [the burden].
Then the moonstone, the shower of nectar, and beyond that, the tiger-seat.
Then Indrāṇī [ascended] the royal throne and likewise the seat of Śarabha.
A jeweled throne with a variegated seat, [and] the bound posture of the Lord of Birds.
The lovely Vicitranalina, Śuddhapakṣī, Sumandraka, Cauraṅgī, as well as Krauñca, Dṛḍhāsana, and Khagāsana.
The Brahmāsana, the Nāgapīṭha, and lastly the Śavāsana. ||3.20||
Thus, when combined, there are eighty-four seats.
Thus, among the pīṭhas mentioned, ten principal ones have been declared.
The Svastika, Gomukha, Padma, Vīra, and likewise Siddhāsana. (3.21)
A peacock, a cock, and likewise an auspicious lion-throne.
Among those, the fourfold Muktāsana is renowned as the foremost. ||3.22||
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*, eighty-four postures were indeed taught by Śiva;
taking from among them a quartet that constitutes the essence, I shall now describe them. (3.23) & HP 1.33
The fourfold [postures] are Siddha, Padma, Siṃha, and Bhadra;
among these, one should always remain in the most excellent, namely, Siddhāsana. (3.24) [Regarding that, Siddhāsana:]
Having firmly placed one foot pressed against the root of the other thigh in the *yoni-sthānaka* posture, and having kept the body perfectly balanced and motionless,
with the senses restrained, he should gaze at the space between the eyebrows with a steady vision like a pillar.
This is declared to be *siddhāsana*, which produces the breaking open of the door of liberation. (3.25) In another tradition, however,
having placed the left ankle above the penis, likewise [the right] above that—
Having placed the two ankles between [the thighs], the perfected ones know this as Siddhāsana.
Some call this Siddhāsana; others know it as Vajrāsana.
Some speak of it as Muktāsana, while others call it Guptāsana.
Living as a celibate student, moderate in diet, renouncing worldly attachments, and devoted to yoga.
After a year, one becomes a Siddha; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
There is no posture equal to *nāsana*, nor is there a *kumbhaka* comparable to *kevala*;
there is no *mudrā* equal to *khecarī*, and no dissolution (*laya*) like that of *nāda*. (3.29)
Then, one should place the two ankles of the *bhadrāsana* below the scrotum and on either side of the perineal seam;
having firmly bound the feet against the sides with the hands, it should be made perfectly motionless.
This is the Bhadrāsana posture; it removes all diseases and poisons.
(3.30) Now, for the Siṃhāsana: one should place the two heels below the scrotum, on either side of the perineum.
The left ankle over the right, and likewise the other over the right. (3.31)
Having placed both hands upon the knees and having fully extended one's own fingers.
With mouth open, one should gaze at the tip of the nose, being fully concentrated.
This shall be the lion-throne, constantly frequented by yogis.
One assumes the supreme posture (*āsana*), which consists of the threefold binding (*bandha-tritaya*). 3.33.
Now, regarding the lotus posture (*padmāsana*):
